evidence: buy(): forwards to this.boxOffice.purchase(eventId, body.email, body.seats) and maps the result to { code, total: euros(result.totalCents) }, so it only delegates and formats
scan(): calls this.boxOffice.admit(body.code) and then this.gates.scanned(ticket.code, body.gate); the admission logic stays in the business layer
events(): maps boxOffice.listing() results to view DTOs, using e.remaining() from the domain and euros() for display
BuyBody/ScanBody interfaces define the shape of request bodies, which is a presentation concern
parsedVerdict.reasoning: TicketController is a thin presentation adapter. It declares request body shapes (BuyBody, ScanBody), hands work to the business services (BoxOffice.purchase, BoxOffice.admit, BoxOffice.listing, GateLog.scanned), and turns the results into response DTOs. It formats cents as euros through the presentation-layer euros helper. It contains no pricing, seat-availability or validation rules. It does no persistence and makes no direct database or storage calls. The one borderline spot is scan(), which calls admit and then gates.scanned in sequence. That is light coordination of two business calls rather than a business rule computed in this file, and it fits a controller's role. Remaining seats come from e.remaining(), a domain method, so the controller does not compute them itself.
